pr_title: expression: refine date_add/sub return type and precision
pr_body:
<!--

Thank you for contributing to TiDB!

PR Title Format:
1. pkg [, pkg2, pkg3]: what's changed
2. *: what's changed

-->

### What problem does this PR solve?
<!--

Please create an issue first to describe the problem.

There MUST be one line starting with "Issue Number:  " and 
linking the relevant issues via the "close" or "ref".

For more info, check https://pingcap.github.io/tidb-dev-guide/contribute-to-tidb/contribute-code.html#referring-to-an-issue.

-->

Issue Number: close #31799, close #9813. And part of #31867 will be resolved by this PR.

Problem Summary:

There exists several issues about function `date_add` and `date_sub`:
1. Return types of several signatures don't match MySQL's [(doc)](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/date-and-time-functions.html#function_date-add):
    1. `date_add/sub(int/double/decimal, interval)`: MySQL returns string, TiDB returns datetime.
    2. `date_add/sub(duration, interval)` when interval unit contains YMD part (except for DAY_MICROSECOND - I believe it's a mismatch between MySQL's actual behavior and its document, but it doesn't matter much), MySQL returns datetime with current date padded, TiDB returns time.
    3. Precision of the return type doesn't match MySQL's in many cases. Note that here I mean the precision concluded by type inference - MySQL client option `--column-type-info` is your good friend.
2. Runtime doesn't respect the precision inferred in compile time. For a datetime value, we check if the MS part is zero then adjust the precision to 0 (min fsp) or 6 (max fsp). No respect to compile time type at all.

Honestly I can file 10+ bugs easily about the above issues.

### What is changed and how it works?

Don't get scared of this huge PR - 90% are tests and 80% of which are generated, the core is quite simple. This PR includes the following changes:
1. The core change is in `expression/builtin_time.go`:
    1. Refine the type inference about the return type and precision of `date_add` and `date_sub`.
    2. Refine the evaluation so that the type and precision by type inference is respected.
    3. Add necessary signatures - ideally we should be able to leverage implicit cast to get a datetime value from int/double/decimal/string, however, as described in this [comment](https://github.com/pingcap/tidb/pull/35009/files#diff-084c9cef9b34d2f1b64570e2cf7d4010b7ce5b26170c480cde3a47441eaa1549R3498), to comply with MySQL's weird behaviors we need specialized overload for each of int/double/decimal/string.
    4. Abstract things like "add or sub", "how to evaluate the datetime value", and "how to evaluate the interval value". Use some simple composition to eliminate the mostly-copy-paste individual overloads. And the overall LOC is reduced from 1456 to 591.
 2. The vectorized versions are simple enough to not use generator, thus moved from generator (expression/generator/time_vec.go) to regular implementations (expression/builtin_time_vec.go). I would have to write more code in template than just directly write them in go. However the vectorized tests are enhanced by adding more cases.
 3. Tests:
     1. Add thorough type infer test cases.
     2. Update several existing UT and integration test cases that already mismatch MySQL's result - each of them is a bug-to-be-reported.
     3. Add more cases to existing UT and integration test.

issue_context.title: `DATE_ADD` function into VARCHAR column returns inconsistent results in fractional portion
issue_context.body:
## Bug Report

Please answer these questions before submitting your issue. Thanks!

### 1. Minimal reproduce step 
```sql
SET @@time_zone='+00:00';
SET @@timestamp=1000000000;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t1; 
CREATE TABLE t1 (a VARCHAR(32));
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(DATE_ADD(CAST('2001-01-01 00:00:00' AS DATETIME), INTERVAL 1 SECOND));
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(DATE_ADD(CAST('2001-01-01 00:00:00' AS DATETIME(6)), INTERVAL 1 SECOND));
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(DATE_ADD(CAST('2001-01-01 00:00:00' AS DATETIME), INTERVAL 1.1 SECOND));
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(DATE_ADD(CAST('2001-01-01 00:00:00' AS DATETIME(6)), INTERVAL 1.1 SECOND));
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(DATE_ADD(CAST('00:00:00' AS TIME), INTERVAL 1.1 SECOND));
SELECT * FROM t1;
DROP TABLE t1;
SET @@timestamp=default;
SET @@time_zone=default;
```

### 2. What did you expect to see?
```sql
mysql> SELECT * FROM t1;
+----------------------------+
| a                          |
+----------------------------+
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01        |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01.000000 |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01.1      |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01.100000 |
| 00:00:01.1                 |
+----------------------------+
```
### 3. What did you see instead 
```sql
tidb> SELECT * FROM t1;
+----------------------------+
| a                          |
+----------------------------+
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01        |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01        |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01.100000 |
| 2001-01-01 00:00:01.100000 |
| 00:00:01                   |
+----------------------------+
```

### 4. What is your TiDB version? 
```
tidb_version(): Release Version: v5.5.0-alpha-105-gaabd4e04d
Edition: Community
Git Commit Hash: aabd4e04d994eb91663abaa80865daec4cf970a6
Git Branch: master
UTC Build Time: 2022-01-13 05:36:36
GoVersion: go1.17.2
Race Enabled: false
TiKV Min Version: v3.0.0-60965b006877ca7234adaced7890d7b029ed1306
Check Table Before Drop: false
```

There are two categories of problems in your reported cases:
1. Precision loss for the fifth row.
2. Precision mismatch between TiDB and MySQL, but not actual loss.

To differentiate these two categories, I'm opening issue https://github.com/pingcap/tidb/issues/34659 to focus on the precision loss, and keeping this one to track the precision mismatch. Also adjusting the severity accordingly.

Why have a fraction on a date? Would not that return a dateTime, since it would infact add a fractional second?

This is not actually a date. It's rather a floating point value that can be recognized by functions like `date_add/sub` as a valid date representation - and the fractional part will be discarded but still is considered valid.

From MySQL:
```
select date_add(cast(20000102.9876 as double), interval 1 second);
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| date_add(cast(20000102.9876 as double), interval 1 second) |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2000-01-02 00:00:01                                        |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
```

This is what this generator is for.
And you can see UT `TestParseTimeFromFloat64` for this usage.

What is the difference between `dateRealGener` and `dateTimeRealGener` then? is both needed? Or should `dateRealGener` only generate a `Float64` that would correspond to a Date and `dateTimeRealGener` generate a `Float64` correspond to a Datetime?

`date/dateTimeDecimalGener` has the same purpose and pattern as `date/dateTimeRealGener` so I'll explain them together here.

`dateReal/DecimalGener` inherits `dateGener`, which generates a date value (a time value with type `mysql.TypeDate`), whose `ToNumber()` method returns a number like `20010203`, i.e., no HMS or us portion.

`dateTimeReal/DecimalGener` inherits `dateTimeGener`, which generates a datetime value (a time value with type `mysql.DateTime`), whose `ToNumber()` method returns a number like `20010203040506.789012`, i.e., with HMS and us portion.

The reason why they are distinguished, is that for functions like `date_add/sub` (and possibly others), when the first argument is a real/decimal value and the second argument is using YMD unit, the return value depends on the content of the first argument (note that the return type is always string - there is no ambiguity about returning date or datetime, and precision). The following statements show this subtle difference:

```
select date_add(20010203.987, interval 1 day);
+----------------------------------------+
| date_add(20010203.987, interval 1 day) |
+----------------------------------------+
| 2001-02-04                             |
+----------------------------------------+

select date_add(20010203040506.987, interval 1 day);
+----------------------------------------------+
| date_add(20010203040506.987, interval 1 day) |
+----------------------------------------------+
| 2001-02-04 04:05:06.987000                   |
+----------------------------------------------+
```

This reveals MySQL must have two different code paths dealing with real/decimal value corresponding to a date and a datetime. So I think both are needed, to explicitly test each code path.

An alternative way would be, combining `dateReal/DecimalGener` and `dateTimeReal/DecimalGener`, and using a dedicated variable to control the ratio of a real/decimal with or w/o HMS portion, i.e., being a date or a datetime. But  I think that's kind of too implicit than the current separated way.
Ah, then I think I understand you, so the fraction part of the `dateRealGener`/`dateDecimalGener` is added just for testing, to be sure that it is never used?
Right. They are for testing only.

I'm afraid this is not valid. There are two type systems in TiDB: "eval type" and "MySQL type". They are for different purpose and not supposed to be mix-used.

Eval type is more like "how data is represented during evaluation", for example, all integer columns, enum columns, and set columns have `ETInt`, and both date and datetime columns have `ETDatetime`.

The examples above reveal exactly the tricks in type inference:
1. Sometimes it is handy to just infer types from eval type - "if this argument has ETInt, no matter it is smallint, bigint, or even enum, the overload is resolved to be this one".
2. Sometimes a function may have a fine-grained type inference rule - "if this argument is date type, the return type is date. If the first argument is datetime type, the return type is datetime". Now the eval type is insufficient. We need to fall back to consulting the mysql type, which is the type specified in the create table statement. And this is what this line does.

Can Timestamp really be possible when returned from Datetime?

It is, in this specific code path. The passing chain of timestamp is:
1. `date_add/sub` is passed the first argument as a timestamp column.
2. In `addSubDateFunctionClass.getFunction`, the eval type for the first argument is chosen to be `types.ETDatetime`. That is, we "treat" timestamp as datetime, no wrapped implicit cast.
3. During evaluation, this function is called by `builtinAddSubDateDatetimeAnySig.vecEvalTime`. Timestamp values are obtained directly from the storage. And `dates[i].Type()` is timestamp.
4. Actually this line is exactly how we "treat" timestamp as datetime.
